title: The economic impact of right-to-work laws: Evidence from collective bargaining agreements and corporate policies
abstract: We analyze the economic and financial impact of right-to-work (RTW) laws in the US. Using data from collective bargaining agreements, we show that there is a decrease in wages for unionized workers after RTW laws. Firms increase investment and employment but reduce financial leverage. Labor-intensive firms experience higher profits and labor-to-asset ratios. Dividends and executive compensation also increase post-RTW. Our results are consistent with a canonical theory of the firm augmented with an exogenous bargaining power of labor and suggest that RTW laws impact corporate policies by decreasing that bargaining power.
summary_en: When US states pass right-to-work (RTW) laws, what happens to wages and corporate behaviour? Chava, Danis and Hsu use data from collective-bargaining agreements and corporate filings to identify the causal impact of state-level RTW adoption. Unionised workers see wages decline. Firms respond by increasing investment and employment but reducing financial leverage. Labour-intensive firms see higher profits and labour-to-asset ratios. Dividends and executive compensation rise. The pattern fits a canonical firm-theory model where RTW reduces labour bargaining power, which in turn reshapes corporate financial decisions.
data_used: Approximately 19,500 US collective-bargaining agreements + Compustat firm financials, covering RTW-adopting and non-adopting states 1998-2016, with state-level RTW timing as the identification source.
policy_relevance: Hungarian labour-policy debates around union bargaining and works-council reforms (e.g., the 2012 Labour Code overhaul) parallel the US RTW question. The paper provides causal evidence that reductions in union bargaining power produce broad corporate-financial responses, not just wage effects — useful framework for the Belügyminisztérium and KSH when assessing distributional impacts of labour-relations reforms.
